1:
The old title attached to this psalm, against Goliath, occupies four of the voices before a word of the text is reached. Keil and Delitzsch report that the Greek version adds it, though on the testimony of an early scholar only in a few copies, and that an Aramaic paraphrast, following a rabbinic source, read the evil sword of the tenth verse as the sword of Goliath. Adam Clarke collects the headings, four versions calling it a psalm of David against Goliath while another says it was made when David slew Asaph the brother of Goliath, and reports Calmet’s guess that it belongs rather to the period after the death of Absalom; he adds that the psalm is an abridgment of an earlier one, preserving the same ideas and forms of expression. John Calvin takes the internal evidence to point past Goliath to the enemies of the kingdom after David came to the throne, and notes that some refer it to the war with the Ammonites and Syrians. Augustine of Hippo keeps the title and reads it as mystery: David put five stones in his scrip and hurled but one, so that the five Books were chosen and unity conquered, and he cut off the giant’s head with the giant’s own sword, as the devil is overthrown with his own weapons when those he held turn their tongues against him.

The first word of the verse divides the expositors. John Gill takes it for the author and giver of natural strength of body, fortitude of mind and spiritual strength alike, and notes that it may be rendered my rock, which three old versions turn into my God. Charles Ellicott prefers rock outright. C.H. Spurgeon allows the reading but objects that it does not consort so well with the teaching of the hands that follows, and Calvin refuses it on the same ground, that the explanation added immediately afterwards is of a man formed for war under God’s teaching; the words imply, he says, that David though of a warlike spirit was not born for warlike enterprises but needed to undergo a change, since his beginning against the giant would have been preposterous on any supposition but that of secret divine support.

On the teaching itself the voices are agreed and various. Spurgeon observes that strength without skill is little gain, since untrained force injures the man who has it and endangers those about him, and that the psalmist therefore blesses God as much for the teaching as for the strength; he adds that not only does the Lord give strength to his saints, he is their strength. Clarke divides the two clauses by weapon, the hands for sword and battle-axe and spear, the fingers for the bow and the sling. Augustine finds a difficulty where others found repetition, and answers that in the fingers we recognise a division of operation with a unity still remaining, as the diversities of operations are all worked by one Spirit. Matthew Henry stands back and looks at the whole opening: a prayer for further mercy is fitly begun with a thanksgiving for former mercy, and David multiplies his words to express what he has, his strength, his goodness, his fortress and high tower, his deliverer, his shield. Henry notices that the third of these is emphatic in the original, a deliverer to him and always near him, and that the man who had sheltered in natural strongholds and had lately taken a fortified one depends on none of them, since the divine attributes and promises are fortifications far exceeding those of nature or art.
2:
The string of titles in the second verse is opened out by two voices. John Gill says the psalmist calls God not only good but goodness itself, and allows the rendering of two old versions, my mercy, or my grace. Charles Ellicott takes it for a shortened form of the phrase God of my grace, exactly analogous to the term grace applied to kings as the source of mercy. On the clause about subduing, he points out that the verb differs from the parallel psalm and that the noun stands here in the singular where the other has peoples; some manuscripts carry the plural and two versions followed them; the incidents out of which the psalm sprang, if we had them, might account for the change. Adam Clarke guesses at a nation once more reduced to obedience, perhaps after the rebellion of Absalom, and John Wesley as God disposing the people’s hearts to receive their king.

The question what man is draws the widest range. Keil and Delitzsch treat it as a variation on an earlier psalm made with other verbs, the word for knowing carrying the sense of loving intimacy, the phrase for the son of man taking an Aramaic form; they remark that the third stanza hangs on the second more loosely still. C.H. Spurgeon makes the contrast the whole point: man is too little to be described at all, too feeble and fickle to be the rock of anyone’s confidence, and the wonder is that God should stoop to know him, more remarkable than if the greatest archangel should study ants or befriend mites. Clarke finds a play in the Hebrew of the next verse, since the word for vanity is the name of Abel, so that man is like to Abel, exposed to the same miseries and murderers, the hands of brothers being lifted to shed the blood of brothers; what are wars, he asks, but fratricide in the great human family? Gill offers the breath of the mouth, after one rabbi, or a vapour. Ellicott admits the occasion for these sentiments is not clear, and offers the humility of a warrior ascribing all success to God, a reflection over the corpses of comrades, or a blending of the two.

With the prayer for God to come down the psalm becomes an echo, and the voices measure the borrowing. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the deeds an earlier psalm celebrates are here turned into petition, that the rescue out of great waters is taken over word for word, and that the enemies are called sons of a foreign country, meaning barbarians; yet so great an imitator, they insist, has much of his own, as the verb for sending forth lightning. Ellicott says the same, that the theophany uses the classic language for such manifestations but with touches of originality, and renders the sixth verse literally as lighten lightning, the verb being peculiar to this place; the word for rid, he adds, means to tear asunder and is used of the gaping of the mouth, its sense here got from cognate languages, and the right hand of falsehood probably alludes to the custom of raising the right hand in an oath. Spurgeon presses the picture: he who exalted the heavens can bow them, the strongest pillars of earth cannot bear the weight of his finger, and if his touch sets the peaks smoking then all mortal power opposed to him must end in smoke. Gill allows a literal sense of clouds hanging low with rain before taking the descent for a manifestation of God, and reports that some read it as a prayer for the incarnation. Wesley keeps the plain sense, that the smoking is like that of the mount at the law-giving, that the strange children are the heathen nations or rebellious countrymen, and that the vanity spoken is vain brags which come to nothing.
9:
The new song becomes for each voice an occasion to say what praise ought to be. John Gill grounds the newness in mercies that are new every morning and so call for a new song continually, and adds that it suits a dispensation in which all things are become new, one Jewish interpreter referring it to the days of the Messiah. Adam Clarke reads new as meaning of peculiar excellence, and undertakes to pour forth all his gratitude and all his skill on the composition. Matthew Henry notes that fresh favours call for fresh returns of thanks, and that we must praise God for mercies hoped for by promise as well as for those received by providence; the ten-stringed instrument comes in because all is little enough for such praise. C.H. Spurgeon makes the newness a turning away: weary of the false he will adore the true, his gratitude cutting a new channel, so that he sings as others have sung and yet what no other has sung.

The instrument then draws from Spurgeon a long qualification, the only extended treatment of music here. He observes that the hand here aids the tongue rather than co-operating in deceit as with the wicked, and that the best instruments are none too good for so great a God. But music, he says, can do no more than represent praise and assist the expression of it, since the real praise is in the heart; the older dispensation abounded in types and outward ritual, and music dropped naturally into place there. His rule follows: when music drowns the voice and artistic skill takes a higher place than hearty singing, it is time that instruments were banished from public worship, but where they stay subordinate to the song it is not for us to prohibit them or condemn those who use them, though he greatly prefers to do without. Charles Ellicott adds a note of a different kind, that the divine name used here is the only instance of it in the last two books of the psalter apart from one psalm which is itself a compilation from two older songs.

Salvation given to kings is the matter of the song, and it is read as a lesson in the limits of power. Henry points out that great kings cannot save themselves: they have life-guards and armies and every device of safety, but it is God who gives them their salvation and could do it without those means; kings protect their people, but God is their protector. Gill puts the same in terms of victory, won not by the force of armies or by military skill but by the right hand of the Lord, and extends the preservation to men and beasts and to those who are kings in a spiritual sense. Clarke takes the verse further than the others and defends the institution: monarchy in principle is from God, it is the form of government which in the course of providence has principally prevailed and which on the whole has been most beneficial to mankind, and God therefore has it under his peculiar protection. Keil and Delitzsch occupy themselves with the word that joins this verse to what follows, which they take to mean because; the Greek version read a different word there, making the following description a picture of the prosperity of the enemies with the possession of the people set against it at the close, and though they grant that this makes the join satisfactorily close, they think it improbable that so carefully drawn a description should belong to the enemies. They add that in the verses following we hear a language altogether peculiar. Gill notes only that the plea for rescue is repeated from earlier in the psalm, to show the vehemence and importunity of the request and the danger the psalmist saw himself in.
12:
The closing picture of prosperity turns on a word no one can construe. Charles Ellicott works through the possibilities, that the relative might be a purpose clause, or mean because, or mean whose, and rejects each on grammatical grounds; there is nothing for it, he concludes, but to treat what follows as a fragment of another poem unconnected with the psalm. John Gill reports the same reading from five old versions, by which the sons and daughters and barns belong to the enemies, and notes that supplying who say turns it into the vain boasting the psalm complained of; but he follows the other versions and takes it for the petition of a good prince. Adam Clarke reads it as neither petition nor boast but inventory, the three promised blessings of the body, the ground and the cattle being actually in possession; the expressions, he insists, should all be understood in the present tense, and a people in such a state who then revolted were doubly guilty, ungrateful to God and man alike.

The images are worked over closely. Ellicott says the word for plants denotes a young vigorous tree lately planted, and that the phrase about their youth must mean grown tall beyond their age or the figure is tame; he prefers a suggested reading of reproductive in their youth, families raised by the young. On the corner stones he notes that the word occurs only once besides, of the corners of an altar, and comes from a root meaning to conceal, as does the word for garners, while the word for polished properly means to hew. C.H. Spurgeon takes the figures for what they teach of a household: the sons matter first to the state, and if they do not grow in youth, when will they; plants may grow crooked, and so may our sons; daughters unite families as corner stones join walls and adorn them as polished stones garnish a building, so that home becomes a palace when the daughters are maids of honour and the sons noble. John Wesley makes the sons the strength and hopes of a nation and the corner stone strong and beautiful.

Ellicott then declares the fourteenth verse full of obscurities. The words rendered oxen strong to labour, he says, can hardly bear that meaning, since the participle is passive; oxen laden with produce, with fat, or with young have all been proposed and all are open to objection. Since the noun elsewhere means heads of families or princes, the participle may mean high in office, and from a cognate form meaning strongly laid offers as his best sense that the line speaks of princes firmly established. For the breaking in he gives a breach in the town walls, two old versions a falling of the fence and others a cattle fold, while Ewald, keeping the pregnant oxen, renders it no abortion and a Syriac version has the cattle great with young and none barren; the going out he takes for war, the complaining for an outcry of sorrow or a battle cry. Clarke reads the same verse as a report on public order, with no robbers or marauding parties and no incursions carrying off property and people, his enemies either become friends or held aloof by fear. Gill and Wesley keep the plainer senses, the oxen burdened with flesh or young, the going out to meet an invader or into captivity. On the last verse Ellicott defends the beatitude: only a narrow and one-sided religion, he says, can see anything out of place in this blessing of plenty and peace, and if we could rejoice with the psalms in temporal blessings without misgiving we should enter the more sincerely into their spiritual depths. Clarke adds that a people so blessed who rebel must have the curse of God and man, while Gill counts the temporal blessings a matter for thankfulness.
